text: RLHF, RLAIF, and Constitutional AI all happen during training. Red-teaming is different — it's adversarial testing on a model that's already trained, deliberately trying to break it before it ships to real users.

Red-teaming means a person or a system deliberately tries to make a model produce outputs its training was meant to prevent, in order to find those gaps before real users do. It's a deployment-time check, not a replacement for training-time alignment work — it assumes that work was imperfect, which, given everything else in this chapter, it reliably is. The name borrows from military exercises, where a red team plays attacker against a defending blue team.

There are two broad approaches. Manual red-teaming uses human testers, who bring creativity and domain judgment but don't scale well — a team can only generate and evaluate so many attempts. Automated red-teaming uses a model to generate adversarial prompts by the thousands, which covers breadth and known variations far faster than people can — but it's weaker at inventing genuinely novel attack ideas nobody has tried yet. Labs typically combine both: automation for scale, people for creativity.

Internal red-teamers know the model and the lab's policies well, but they also share the lab's own blind spots about what a normal user would try. External, third-party testers bring different backgrounds, different professional contexts, and different assumptions about use, which is why frontier labs run outside red-teaming programs alongside their internal ones.

Red-teaming doesn't train the model — it finds where training didn't work, and those findings feed back into further training, new refusal behaviors, or policy changes. Next lesson: the specific jailbreak techniques red-teaming is looking for, and why they can work at all.
